2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation
A company is concerned that committing to a single model provider will leave it stuck if better or cheaper models appear. Which strategy best reduces this lock-in risk?
Sign a 10-year exclusive contract with one provider for the best discount
Avoid all generative AI until the market consolidates
Build every model in-house to avoid vendors
Use a platform that offers choice across multiple models and keep data, prompts, and evaluations portable
A multi-model platform, which is how Amazon Bedrock is positioned, plus portable assets lets the company switch models as the market changes.
Long exclusive contracts increase lock-in, waiting gives up value, and building everything in-house is costly and creates a different kind of dependency.
2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation

A procurement team is evaluating a third-party generative AI SaaS product that will process customer data. Which TWO due-diligence questions matter most? Pick the pair of correct statements.  (1) What color themes does the interface support?.  (2) Will our data be used to train the vendor's models, and where is it stored and processed?.  (3) How many employees does the vendor have on social media?.  (4) Does the vendor have a mascot?.  (5) What security and compliance certifications does the vendor hold, and does it offer IP indemnity for outputs?.
Buying AI means inheriting the vendor's data practices and risks.

Data use and residency, security and compliance attestations, and intellectual-property protections are critical. Interface themes, social media headcount, and branding have no bearing on risk or fit.
2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation
A company has decided to buy a third-party AI document-processing solution. It wants to simplify procurement and have the charges appear on its existing AWS bill. Where should it look?
AWS Marketplace is a catalog of third-party software, including AI products, models, and data, with procurement and billing consolidated through AWS.
Cost Explorer analyzes spending, SageMaker AI is for building ML models, and the Pricing Calculator estimates costs before you build.
2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation

A bank learns that a competitor will launch an AI-powered mortgage pre-approval experience in three months. Building a comparable solution internally would take 12 months. A proven vendor solution can be integrated in about 10 weeks and meets the bank's compliance requirements. Which factor most favors buying here?
Buying is always cheaper than building
Time to value: buying lets the bank respond to the competitive threat in time
Building would give the bank more control over everything
When speed matters competitively and a compliant solution exists, time to value can decide build vs.
buy. Buying isn't always cheaper, vendors do carry risks that need due diligence, and while building offers control, that argues *for* building, not buying.
2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation

A European healthcare provider wants a clinical documentation assistant. The leading SaaS product can't guarantee that patient data stays within the EU, which the provider's data residency rules require. The provider has a small cloud team but no ML researchers. What's the best approach?
Buy the SaaS anyway and accept the compliance gap
Build on a managed foundation-model platform in an EU AWS Region, using managed services so no model training is needed, possibly with a partner's help
Train a proprietary clinical foundation model from scratch

Data residency rules out the SaaS product, and a lack of ML researchers rules out training a model. A hybrid build on managed services in a compliant Region meets residency needs with a small team, and a partner can speed delivery. Accepting the gap creates regulatory exposure, and abandoning the initiative gives up the value.
2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation
A support director plans to launch an AI assistant next month and prove its value to finance six months later. What must the team do *before* launch?
Measure the current baseline, for example average handle time, cost per contact, and customer satisfaction
Nothing, since savings will be obvious afterward
Ask the vendor to provide the ROI figure
You can't prove improvement without a "before" measurement.
A baseline taken before launch is the anchor for every KPI and ROI claim. Waiting until afterward loses the comparison, and an ROI figure from the vendor isn't independent evidence.
2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation
An AI document-processing program costs $200,000 in its first year, including licenses, integration, and training. It produces $500,000 in measured first-year benefits. What is the first-year ROI?
The 250% figure divides benefit by cost without subtracting the cost first. The 60% and 40% figures divide by the benefit instead of the cost.
2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation
Three months into a sales-copilot rollout, revenue impact can't be measured yet. Which metric is the best *leading* indicator that the initiative is on track?
Weekly active usage of the copilot among target sales reps
Leading indicators, such as adoption, usage, and user satisfaction, give early signals.
If people don't use the tool, no value will follow. Revenue, margin, and lifetime value are lagging indicators that show results only after months or years.
2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation

An AI tool saves each of 100 claims processors about 90 minutes a day. The business case counts this as "$2 million in annual savings." Headcount, overtime, and work volume all stay the same. What's the main problem with this claim?
Freed time is a soft saving that only becomes value if it's redeployed, for example to more claims, faster settlement, or less overtime

Soft savings free up capacity. If nothing changes in output, cost, or quality, the freed time produces no measurable value. Strong business cases say how the capacity will be redeployed and track that outcome.
2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation
An AI initiative requires a $300,000 upfront investment and produces a net benefit of $25,000 per month after running costs. What is the payback period?
Payback period = upfront investment ÷ monthly net benefit = $300,000 ÷ $25,000 = 12 months.
Executives often use payback alongside ROI to judge how quickly an investment recovers its cost.
2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation

Online sales rose 8% in the month an AI product-recommendation engine launched. The same month also had a holiday promotion and a competitor's outage. How can the team best attribute the lift to the AI?
Credit all 8% to the AI, since it launched that month
Compare a randomly assigned group that saw AI recommendations with a control group that didn't (an A/B test)
Ask customers whether they noticed the AI
Credit none of it, since attribution is impossible
Control groups separate the AI's effect from other factors, such as promotions, seasonality, and competitor events.
Crediting all of the lift to the AI is false attribution, customer surveys can't measure the causal impact, and attribution is very possible with good experiment design.
2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation
A data science team reports to the executive committee that the new fraud model's F1 score improved from 0.71 to 0.84. Executives ask, "So what?" Which KPI would communicate value best?
Precision and recall reported to four decimal places
Fraud losses avoided per month and the reduction in legitimate transactions wrongly declined
Executives need business KPIs: money saved, customer friction reduced, risk lowered.
Model metrics like F1, precision, and recall matter to technical teams but should be translated into business outcomes. Parameter counts and training time say nothing about value.
2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation

A business case for a generative AI assistant includes only the model's usage fees. Which TWO commonly overlooked costs should be added? Pick the pair of correct statements.  (1) Change management and user training.  (2) The color of the office walls.  (3) Executives' personal phone plans.  (4) Data preparation and integration with existing systems.  (5) Competitors' marketing budgets.
Model fees are often a small part of the total cost of ownership.
Data preparation, integration, security, monitoring, and the people side (training and change management) are frequently larger. The other options have nothing to do with the initiative's cost.
2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation
A startup is piloting a generative AI feature. It has no idea whether usage will be 1,000 or 100,000 requests a month. Which pricing approach best fits this stage?
Seat-based licenses for every possible user
Consumption-based (on-demand) pricing, paying per token or request
When demand is uncertain or variable, pay-as-you-go pricing avoids paying for idle capacity and scales with real usage.
Commitments, dedicated hardware, and per-seat licenses all assume demand you can't yet predict.
2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation

A large insurer's generative AI claims assistant now handles a steady, predictable, high volume of requests around the clock. Performance must be consistent at peak times. Which Amazon Bedrock pricing option fits best?
Provisioned Throughput, which reserves dedicated model capacity for a term
Provisioned Throughput reserves model capacity, giving consistent performance for steady, high-volume production, and longer commitments lower the hourly rate.
On-demand suits variable workloads. Batch suits non-urgent bulk jobs, not real-time assistance, and a free tier isn't a production option.
2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation
Each night, a bank needs to summarize 200,000 archived documents for a compliance review. Results are needed by the next morning, not in real time. Which approach most reduces cost?
Real-time on-demand calls, one document at a time
Batch inference, which processes requests in bulk at a lower price than on-demand for supported models
The largest available model for every document
For large jobs that aren't urgent, batch inference is far cheaper.
On Amazon Bedrock it's priced well below on-demand for supported models. Real-time calls cost more without any benefit here, the largest model raises cost, and temperature has no effect on price.
2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation

A retailer uses the largest, most capable foundation model to classify customer emails into five categories. An evaluation shows a much smaller model reaches the same accuracy on this task at a fraction of the cost per request. What should the retailer do?
Keep the largest model, because bigger is always safer
Use both models on every email
Right-size by switching this task to the smaller model, and keep monitoring quality
Choosing the smallest model that meets the quality bar is one of the biggest generative AI cost levers.
Simple tasks rarely need the most powerful model. Running both models doubles cost, and dropping the task gives up its value.
2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation
After launch, a CFO wants to see actual month-by-month AWS spending on the company's generative AI projects, with trends and breakdowns by project. Which tool fits best?
AWS Cost Explorer, with cost allocation tags for each project
Cost Explorer analyzes *actual* spending and trends, and tags let costs be broken down by project.
The Pricing Calculator estimates costs *before* building, Marketplace is for buying third-party software, and SageMaker AI is an ML platform.
2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation
A vendor's sales deck promises "40% productivity gains" from its AI writing tool, based on studies at other companies. The CFO wants to use 40% in the investment case. What's the most sound approach?
Run a measured pilot against the company's own baseline and base the business case on observed results, with conservative assumptions
Use 40%, since the vendor's studies are published
Double it to 80% to be ambitious
Use 0% because vendor claims are always false
Results depend on context: workflows, users, data, and adoption.

A pilot measured against your own baseline gives credible figures, and conservative assumptions protect the business case. Adopting, inflating, or dismissing the vendor's figure without evidence are all weak practice.
2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation
Every competitor in an industry can access the same leading foundation models through cloud platforms. Where is a company's *durable* AI competitive advantage most likely to come from?
Being the only company using a specific public model
Proprietary data, deep integration into its own workflows, and customer experience, all of which competitors can't easily copy
Spending the most on model usage fees
Foundation models are increasingly a commodity anyone can rent.

Advantage comes from what others can't replicate: unique data (a "data moat"), processes redesigned around AI, and a better customer experience. Exclusive model access is rare and short-lived, and spending or announcements don't create an edge.
2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation
An online retailer uses AI to tailor homepage products and email offers to each shopper's browsing and purchase history. Conversion rates rise 12%. Which type of AI value does this mainly represent?
Improved customer experience and revenue through personalization
Personalization improves relevance for customers and drives revenue through higher conversion.
Operational efficiency would mean cutting cost or time in internal processes. Compliance and infrastructure cost aren't what this example delivers.
2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation

An agricultural-equipment maker starts selling farmers a subscription service that uses AI on sensor data from their machines to predict crop yields and recommend planting schedules. Which kind of AI value does this represent?
Business model innovation: a new revenue stream built on AI and data
Moving from one-time equipment sales to an AI-powered recurring service changes how the company makes money.
That's business model innovation, the highest-value and highest-uncertainty kind of AI transformation. The other options describe internal improvements.
2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation

Which TWO are the strongest sources of sustainable competitive advantage from AI? Pick the pair of correct statements.  (1) Using the same off-the-shelf chatbot as every competitor.  (2) Unique, high-quality proprietary data that improves the AI over time.  (3) A press release announcing an "AI-first" strategy.  (4) The largest number of AI pilots, regardless of results.  (5) AI embedded into redesigned core processes that competitors would struggle to replicate.
Proprietary data and deep process integration are hard to copy and get stronger over time.
Off-the-shelf tools give parity, not advantage. Announcements and pilot counts don't create lasting value.
2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation

A mid-market manufacturer is deciding whether to be first in its industry to deploy AI-generated supplier contract summaries, a useful but non-core back-office capability. Proven solutions are emerging fast. What's the most sensible stance?
Fast follower: adopt proven solutions once they mature, saving pioneering effort for capabilities that differentiate the business
First mover at any cost, building a custom solution now
Never adopt it, because back-office AI has no value
For non-core capabilities, being a fast follower lowers risk and cost while still capturing value.
Being first matters most where the capability is a real differentiator. Refusing or waiting a decade gives up clear efficiency gains.
2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation

A bank added a generative AI assistant to its loan-processing workflow, but the 11-step process, handoffs, and approval rules stayed exactly the same. Loan cycle time improved only 3%. What best explains the limited impact?
The foundation model is too small
The value of AI depends on redesigning the process around it; adding AI to an unchanged workflow limits the gains
Generative AI can't help in banking
The assistant needs a higher temperature
Transformational value usually comes from rethinking the workflow: removing steps, changing handoffs, and moving people to exception handling.
AI layered onto a legacy process inherits its bottlenecks. Model size and temperature aren't the limiting factors, and banking has many proven AI uses.
2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation
A delivery company uses AI to optimize daily routes. Fuel use and driver overtime fall 14% with no change to the service customers receive. Which kind of AI value is this mainly?
Getting the same output for less cost or time is operational efficiency, the most common early source of AI value.
No new business model, revenue stream, or brand effect is involved.
2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation

A retail chain's regional managers set inventory levels by gut feel. Leadership deploys an AI tool that shows demand forecasts, what-if scenarios, and recommended stock levels, while managers still make the final call. How does AI create value here?
By eliminating the need for inventory
By improving the quality and speed of human decisions with better information
Better decision-making is a core AI value lever.
AI provides forecasts and scenarios, and people apply judgment and accountability. The managers stay in place, inventory still matters, and cloud cost isn't the point.
2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation
A competitor announces a flashy AI avatar for its mobile app. The CEO asks the team to "build the same thing by next quarter." What's the strategist's best response?
Build an identical avatar immediately to keep up
Copy the competitor's entire AI roadmap
Assess whether the feature addresses real customer needs and fits the company's strategy before deciding to follow, differentiate, or skip
Competitive moves should be weighed against your own customers' needs, your strategy, and the evidence of value.
Reflexive copying wastes money on features that may not matter. Ignoring competitors forever is complacent, and copying a whole roadmap gives up your own direction.
2. AI Strategy and Business Value Creation

A software company's AI self-service assistant resolves most customer issues. That reduces demand for its paid "premium support" tier, a meaningful revenue line. How should leadership evaluate the initiative?
Cancel it to protect premium support revenue
Assess the net impact: lost support revenue against gains in customer satisfaction, retention, lower support costs, and possible new premium offerings
Hide the assistant from premium customers
Raise premium support prices to compensate

Strategic evaluation looks at the whole picture, because if the company doesn't offer a better experience, a competitor will. Cancelling or hiding the assistant protects short-term revenue at long-term cost, and price hikes ignore the change in what customers value.
3. AI Governance and Responsible AI Leadership

An audit finds that a lender's AI approves applicants from certain postal codes at much lower rates than similarly qualified applicants elsewhere. The postal codes correlate strongly with ethnicity. Which responsible AI dimension is most at stake?
Fairness means AI outcomes don't unjustly disadvantage groups.
Proxy variables such as postal code can bring in discrimination even when protected attributes are excluded. The other dimensions cover human control, reliable outputs, and openness about AI use.
3. AI Governance and Responsible AI Leadership
A customer whose credit-line increase was declined by an AI system asks, "Why was I turned down?" Which responsible AI dimension lets the company give a meaningful answer?
Explainability is the ability to understand and communicate *why* the AI produced a particular output, such as the factors that drove a decision.
Safety prevents harm, controllability keeps humans able to steer the AI, and privacy protects data.
3. AI Governance and Responsible AI Leadership

A telecom company's support chat is now handled by a generative AI assistant, but customers aren't told, and many believe they're chatting with a person. Which responsible AI principle does this most directly undermine?
Transparency means being open about when and how AI is used, including telling people they're talking to an AI.
It builds trust, and some regulations require it. Fairness, robustness, and cost aren't the main issue in this scenario.
3. AI Governance and Responsible AI Leadership

A logistics company insists that operators must be able to override its AI dispatch system's decisions and shut it down immediately if it misbehaves. Which responsible AI dimension does this requirement address?
Controllability is the ability to monitor and steer AI behavior, including overrides, fallbacks, and kill switches.
Fairness concerns equal treatment, explainability concerns understanding outputs, and veracity concerns correctness.
3. AI Governance and Responsible AI Leadership

An insurance chatbot works well in testing. In production, it gives wrong answers when customers make typos, use slang, or ask unusual multi-part questions. Which responsible AI dimension needs strengthening?
Veracity and robustness mean producing correct outputs even with unexpected, noisy, or adversarial inputs.
Testing should cover realistic edge cases, not just clean examples. The other dimensions don't address reliability under messy real-world inputs.
3. AI Governance and Responsible AI Leadership

A marketing team wants to send full customer records, including names, addresses, birth dates, and purchase histories, to a generative AI model to write campaign copy. The copy only needs general segment preferences. What responsible AI practice applies?
Data minimization: send only the data the task needs, and remove or mask personal details
Send everything, since more data always improves output
Send the data to as many models as possible to compare results
Privacy and security include using only the minimum data needed.

Segment-level preferences meet the need without exposing personal details. More data isn't always better, spreading data across many models increases exposure, and cancelling the campaign is unnecessary.
3. AI Governance and Responsible AI Leadership

An education company is launching a generative AI homework helper for a broad public audience. Which responsible AI dimension calls most directly for filters that block violent, self-harm, or otherwise harmful content?
Safety is about preventing harmful outputs and misuse, especially for vulnerable audiences.
Content filters and guardrails, such as Amazon Bedrock Guardrails, are the main controls. The other options don't address harmful content.
3. AI Governance and Responsible AI Leadership

For a regulated small-business lending decision, the data science team presents two models. One is a complex model with 2% higher accuracy but limited interpretability. The other is an interpretable model whose decision factors can be clearly explained. Regulators require specific reasons for every decline. Which choice best reflects responsible AI leadership?
The complex model, because accuracy always wins
Deploy both and let customers choose
The interpretable model, accepting a small accuracy trade-off to meet explainability and regulatory requirements, and documenting the decision
Neither, so the lender stops lending to small businesses
Responsible AI often means weighing trade-offs openly, such as accuracy against explainability.

When regulation and fairness require explanations, a small accuracy gain doesn't justify losing them. Documenting the trade-off is part of governance. Letting customers choose models makes no sense, and abandoning the market is unnecessary.
3. AI Governance and Responsible AI Leadership

A company wants to check a hiring-support model for bias before launch. Which TWO practices help most? Pick the pair of correct statements.  (1) Use bias-detection tooling, such as Amazon SageMaker Clarify, to measure outcome differences across groups.  (2) Remove all testing to speed up launch.  (3) Test only on data from the company's current employees.  (4) Evaluate the model on diverse, representative data that reflects the full applicant population.  (5) Rely on the vendor's statement that the model is "unbiased".
Measuring outcome differences with bias tools, and testing on representative data, are core fairness practices.
Testing only on current employees repeats historical bias, skipping testing is negligent, and vendor claims need independent verification.
3. AI Governance and Responsible AI Leadership
A project team says responsible AI was "handled" because an ethics committee approved the project once, at kickoff. What's wrong with this view?
Ethics committees should never review AI
Responsible AI applies across the whole lifecycle (design, data, testing, deployment, and ongoing monitoring), because risks change as data, users, and models change
Responsible AI only matters after a public incident
Risks such as drift, emerging bias, and new misuse patterns appear after launch.
Responsible AI is a continuous lifecycle practice, not a single checkpoint. Committee review is useful but not enough on its own, and waiting for an incident is reactive.
3. AI Governance and Responsible AI Leadership

On a previous AI project, legal and security reviewed the solution only one week before launch. They found serious issues, and the launch slipped four months. What practice would prevent this next time?
Skip legal and security reviews to protect timelines
Have legal and security review only after launch
Governance by design: involve legal, security, risk, and privacy from the start and build their requirements into the design
Hire more developers to move faster
Building governance in from the start catches issues when they're cheap to fix, and it often speeds delivery overall.
Skipping reviews or postponing them until after launch shifts risk into production, and adding developers doesn't fix late-stage compliance gaps.
3. AI Governance and Responsible AI Leadership
A company is forming an AI governance council to approve and oversee AI initiatives. Which membership is most effective?
Cross-functional: business leaders plus legal, compliance and risk, security, data, technology, and HR representatives
AI risks and value span many functions: legal, ethical, security, data, people, and business outcomes.
Cross-functional governance brings all those views together. A single-function council has blind spots, and vendors have conflicts of interest.
3. AI Governance and Responsible AI Leadership
Why should an organization maintain an AI inventory, also called an AI registry?
To count how many GPUs it owns
To list employees' favorite AI websites
To replace the need for any AI policy
To keep a central record of every AI system in use, with its owner, purpose, data, risk level, and status, so it can be governed
You can't govern what you can't see.

An AI inventory shows what exists, who owns it, what data it touches, and how risky it is, and it helps uncover shadow AI. It isn't a hardware count or a list of favorite sites, and it supports policy rather than replacing it.
3. AI Governance and Responsible AI Leadership
A business team wants to understand a model's intended uses, limitations, performance characteristics, and responsible AI considerations before adopting it. Which documentation is designed for this?
A model card (AWS publishes AI Service Cards for its AI services)
Model cards and AWS AI Service Cards document intended use, limitations, performance, and responsible AI design, which supports transparency and informed adoption.
Invoices and brochures don't cover this, and source code isn't written for business readers.
3. AI Governance and Responsible AI Leadership

An AI system wrongly denies a batch of legitimate warranty claims. In the post-incident review, the business, data science, and vendor teams each say "the AI made the decision." What governance gap does this reveal?
The vendor should be solely responsible
There was no clearly named accountable owner for the AI system's outcomes
AI decisions can never be audited

Every AI system needs a named business owner who is accountable for its outcomes, supported by clear roles (for example, a RACI chart). "The AI did it" is never acceptable. Model size is irrelevant, vendors share but don't absorb accountability, and AI decisions can be audited with proper logging.
3. AI Governance and Responsible AI Leadership

A company's single, heavyweight AI approval process takes 10 weeks for every request, from an internal meeting-summary tool to an AI that sets insurance premiums. Teams are bypassing it. Which TWO changes reflect effective, risk-based governance? Pick the pair of correct statements.  (1) Low-risk uses (internal, non-sensitive, human-reviewed) get a streamlined, fast-track approval.  (2) Remove governance entirely to restore speed.  (3) Apply the full 10-week process to everything, but more strictly.  (4) High-risk uses (affecting customers' rights, finances, or safety) get deeper review, including an impact assessment.  (5) Let each team decide whether governance applies to it.
Matching controls to risk lets governance enable speed for low-risk uses while focusing rigor where harm is possible.
One-size-fits-all processes drive teams to bypass them, removing governance invites incidents, and self-exemption isn't governance.
3. AI Governance and Responsible AI Leadership
A company builds a RACI chart for its AI customer-service assistant. Which role means "the single person who ultimately answers for the outcome and signs off"?
"Accountable" is the one owner who answers for the outcome, usually a business leader for an AI system.
"Responsible" means the people doing the work, "Consulted" means those whose input is sought, and "Informed" means those kept up to date.
3. AI Governance and Responsible AI Leadership
A regulator asks a bank to show exactly how its AI system reached a specific loan decision 18 months ago. Which governance capability makes this possible?
An audit trail that logs the inputs, model version, output, any human review, and approvals for each decision
Audit trails, together with model versioning, let organizations reconstruct and justify past AI decisions, which is essential for regulated use.
A newer model can't explain an old decision, and marketing materials and memories aren't evidence.
3. AI Governance and Responsible AI Leadership

An internal review finds that a pricing model "replaced" two years ago is still quietly running inside an old reporting app. It's making outdated recommendations that some managers still use. Which governance gap does this reveal?
Governance that doesn't cover the full lifecycle, including formal retirement and decommissioning of AI systems
Lifecycle governance runs from idea to retirement.
Without formal decommissioning tied to an AI inventory, old models linger and create risk. Documentation, model size, and oversight levels aren't the cause here.
3. AI Governance and Responsible AI Leadership
A bank applies the "three lines of defense" model to AI. Which role does the *second* line play?
Building and operating the AI systems day to day
Risk and compliance oversight: setting AI risk policies, challenging the first line, and monitoring adherence
The first line, the business and its delivery teams, owns and manages the risk.
The second line, risk and compliance, sets policy and oversees it. The third line, internal audit, provides independent assurance. Sales isn't part of the model.
3. AI Governance and Responsible AI Leadership
Under a risk-tiered AI regulation such as the EU AI Act, which use is most likely to be classified as *high-risk* and subject to strict requirements?
An AI system that screens job applicants or evaluates creditworthiness
A spam filter for internal email
An AI that suggests playlist songs
A grammar checker for marketing drafts
Risk-tiered regulation puts AI that affects people's access to jobs, credit, education, or essential services in the high-risk category.
Those uses require risk management, data governance, documentation, human oversight, and transparency. The other examples are minimal-risk uses.
3. AI Governance and Responsible AI Leadership
A multinational's legal team distinguishes "data residency" from "data sovereignty" when planning an AI deployment. Which statement is correct?
Data residency concerns which country's laws apply; data sovereignty concerns where data is physically stored
Data residency concerns where data is physically stored; data sovereignty concerns which country's laws and authorities govern the data
Residency is about physical location, for example choosing an AWS Region.
Sovereignty is about legal jurisdiction over the data. Both shape where and how AI workloads can run. Option B reverses the definitions, and both concepts apply fully to AI.
3. AI Governance and Responsible AI Leadership

A company builds a generative AI application on Amazon Bedrock. Under the AWS shared responsibility model, which TWO are the *customer's* responsibility? Pick the pair of correct statements.  (1) Physical security of AWS data centers.  (2) Configuring access controls so only authorized users and applications can use the AI and its data.  (3) Patching the hardware that hosts the foundation models.  (4) Deciding what data goes into prompts and knowledge bases, and how the AI's outputs are used.  (5) Maintaining the global network infrastructure.
AWS secures the cloud itself: facilities, hardware, network, and the managed service.

Customers secure what they put *in* the cloud and how they use it: identity and access, their data, prompts, outputs, and use-case decisions. Data centers, hardware patching, and the global network belong to AWS.
3. AI Governance and Responsible AI Leadership
Which of the following is AWS's responsibility, not the customer's, when a company uses Amazon Bedrock?
Writing the company's acceptable use policy for AI
Securing the infrastructure and managed service that host and run the foundation models
Deciding which employees may access customer data
Reviewing AI outputs before they're sent to customers
AWS is responsible for the security *of* the cloud, including the infrastructure and managed service behind Bedrock.
Policies, access decisions, and reviewing outputs are the customer's responsibilities.
3. AI Governance and Responsible AI Leadership

A call center wants to use generative AI to summarize customer calls. The transcripts contain names, phone numbers, and account numbers that the summaries don't need. Which control best supports compliance?
Store the transcripts in more places for redundancy
Detect and redact or mask personally identifiable information before or during processing, for example with Amazon Bedrock Guardrails' sensitive-information filters
Email the transcripts to the vendor for manual review
Redacting PII applies data minimization and lowers privacy and compliance risk.
Guardrails and services such as Amazon Comprehend can detect and mask sensitive information. Extra copies and emailing transcripts increase exposure, and temperature has nothing to do with privacy.
3. AI Governance and Responsible AI Leadership

A utility company collected customers' usage data for billing. The marketing team now wants to use the same data to train an AI model that predicts which customers will buy solar panels. What should happen first?
Use the data immediately, since the company already has it
Buy external data instead without any review
Check with legal and privacy whether this new purpose is permitted under the original consent or lawful basis, and get consent or adjust if needed
Privacy laws often limit data to the purposes it was collected for.

Reusing data for a new AI purpose may need fresh consent or a different lawful basis. Having the data doesn't mean you're allowed to use it this way, deleting billing data is extreme, and external data needs review too.
3. AI Governance and Responsible AI Leadership
A CISO hesitates to approve Amazon Bedrock, asking, "Will our prompts and data be used to train the foundation models or be shared with the model providers?" What's the accurate answer?
No. With Amazon Bedrock, customer prompts and outputs aren't used to train the base models and aren't shared with third-party model providers
Yes. All prompts are shared publicly
Yes. Model providers receive all prompts to improve their models
It depends on the font used in the prompts
AWS states that Bedrock doesn't use customer prompts or outputs to train its base models and doesn't share them with model providers.
Combined with encryption and access controls, this addresses a common executive concern about enterprise generative AI. The other answers are false.
3. AI Governance and Responsible AI Leadership

Employees ask which company information they may use with the approved AI assistant. The company labels data as Public, Internal, Confidential, and Restricted. What's the most effective way to guide them?
Allow all data in all AI tools
Tie the AI acceptable-use policy to data classification, specifying which classes may be used in which approved tools, and train staff on it
Ban all data from all AI tools
Let each employee decide case by case without guidance
Linking AI use to existing data classification gives clear, scalable rules.

For example, Restricted data may be used only in specific approved, isolated tools. All-or-nothing rules either create risk or block value, and leaving it to each employee produces inconsistent, risky behavior.
3. AI Governance and Responsible AI Leadership

A European insurer wants AI to fully automate decisions on whether to pay claims, with no human involvement. Privacy regulation gives individuals rights regarding decisions based solely on automated processing that significantly affect them. What design best supports compliance?
Fully automate and don't tell customers
Provide meaningful human review for significant decisions (especially denials), explain the decision logic, and give customers a way to contest outcomes
Move the data to another country to avoid the regulation
GDPR-style rules on automated decisions point toward human involvement, transparency about the logic, and a way for people to challenge outcomes.
AI can still triage and recommend. Hiding automation breaks transparency, abandoning AI gives up value, and moving data abroad doesn't remove the obligations.
3. AI Governance and Responsible AI Leadership

An airline's website chatbot invents a bereavement-fare refund policy. A tribunal later rules that the airline must honor what its chatbot told the customer. Which combination of controls best reduces this risk?
A higher temperature, for more natural conversation
Removing the chatbot's access to all company documents
Telling customers that chatbot answers are "probably right"
Grounding answers in approved policy documents (RAG), requiring citations, blocking unsupported policy claims with guardrails, and escalating policy questions to humans
Hallucinations create legal and financial liability.

Layered controls address both the cause and the impact: grounding, citations, guardrails such as contextual grounding checks, and human escalation. Higher temperature increases fabrication, removing document access makes it worse, and a vague disclaimer won't shield the company from liability.
3. AI Governance and Responsible AI Leadership
A company trains a résumé-screening model on 10 years of past hiring decisions. Historically, most hires came from a narrow set of universities and backgrounds. What risk is most likely?
Historical bias: the model learns and repeats past patterns, unfairly disadvantaging qualified candidates from other backgrounds
Models learn from historical decisions, including their biases.
Without bias testing and correction, AI can automate past discrimination at scale. Hallucination, cost, and prompt injection aren't the main concern in this scenario.
3. AI Governance and Responsible AI Leadership

A marketing team uses an image-generation tool to create campaign visuals. Legal worries that some outputs may closely resemble copyrighted characters or another brand's trademarks. Which approach best manages this intellectual property risk?
Use any generated image, since AI outputs can't infringe
Ban all generative AI in marketing permanently
Use approved tools whose providers offer IP indemnity where available, add human legal or brand review before publishing, and avoid prompts that reference protected works
Add a watermark that says "AI-generated" and publish everything
IP risk is managed through vendor protections, review processes, and prompt guidance.
AI outputs *can* infringe, a permanent ban gives up value, and a watermark discloses AI use but doesn't fix infringement.
3. AI Governance and Responsible AI Leadership
An attacker secretly inserts manipulated records into data that will be used to train a company's fraud model, so that certain fraudulent patterns are learned as "safe." What is this attack called?
Data poisoning corrupts training data to manipulate model behavior.
Defenses include securing data pipelines, controlling access, tracking where data came from, and validating data. Hallucination, drift, and overfitting aren't deliberate attacks.
3. AI Governance and Responsible AI Leadership

After a year with an AI underwriting assistant, reviewers approve its recommendations 99% of the time, often within seconds and without opening the supporting documents. Several costly errors have slipped through. What risk is this?
Automation bias (over-reliance), where humans trust AI outputs without proper scrutiny
Human review only works if it's real.

Automation bias turns oversight into rubber-stamping. Countermeasures include training, review checklists, sampling audits, showing the AI's confidence, and periodic "challenge" cases. The other options are technical issues, not human-behavior risks.
3. AI Governance and Responsible AI Leadership

A bank is about to launch a public-facing generative AI assistant. Before going live, it hires a team to try to make the assistant reveal confidential data, produce harmful content, and ignore its rules. What is this practice called?
Red teaming deliberately attacks an AI system to find vulnerabilities such as jailbreaks, data leaks, and harmful outputs before real attackers do.
A/B testing compares variants for business impact, fine-tuning customizes a model, and labeling prepares training data.
3. AI Governance and Responsible AI Leadership

A company is building an AI risk register for its generative AI portfolio. Which TWO elements should each entry include? Pick the pair of correct statements.  (1) The model's marketing tagline.  (2) A named risk owner and the planned mitigation or controls.  (3) The favorite AI tool of the project sponsor.  (4) The risk's likelihood and potential impact, used to prioritize it.  (5) The number of social media posts about the risk.
A useful risk register records each risk's owner, likelihood and impact, mitigations, and status, so risks can be prioritized and tracked over time.
Taglines, personal preferences, and social media counts aren't risk-management information.
3. AI Governance and Responsible AI Leadership

Users of a retailer's public shopping assistant share tricks online for getting it to ignore its rules, for example role-play prompts that make it write offensive jokes about competitors. What is this, and what's the best response?
Data poisoning; delete the training data
Jailbreaking; strengthen guardrails, monitor for abuse patterns, and update defenses as new techniques appear
Jailbreaks trick a model into bypassing its safety instructions.
Defense is ongoing: layered guardrails such as input and output filters and denied topics, plus abuse monitoring and regular updates. Drift, poisoning, and overfitting are different problems.
3. AI Governance and Responsible AI Leadership
Engineers at a manufacturer paste proprietary source code and chip designs into a free public chatbot to get debugging help. What's the primary risk?
Confidential data leaking outside the company's control, with possible loss of trade secrets
Higher GPU costs for the company
Sending confidential IP to unapproved public tools can expose it beyond the company's control, depending on the provider's terms.
This is a classic shadow AI risk, and the remedy is approved enterprise tools plus policy and training. The other options aren't the main concern.
3. AI Governance and Responsible AI Leadership

After applying guardrails, grounding, and human review to a marketing content assistant, a small *residual* risk of occasional off-brand phrasing remains. The business considers this tolerable. What's the correct governance step?
Hide the residual risk from leadership
Keep adding controls until risk is exactly zero
Cancel the project, because some risk remains
Have the accountable owner formally accept the residual risk, document it in the risk register, and continue monitoring

Governance means risk is reduced to a level within tolerance, then accepted by an authorized owner, documented, and monitored. Hiding the risk breaks accountability, chasing zero wastes resources, and cancelling ignores the risk appetite.
3. AI Governance and Responsible AI Leadership

A company proposes an AI feature that would infer customers' health conditions from their shopping patterns to target ads. Legal and ethics reviews conclude the privacy and reputational risks can't be reduced to an acceptable level. Which risk treatment fits best?
Accept the risk and launch quietly
Avoid the risk by not building the feature, and redirect effort to lower-risk personalization
Transfer the risk entirely by buying insurance
Mitigate it by adding a small disclaimer in the privacy policy
When a risk can't be brought within tolerance, avoiding it, by not doing the activity, is the right treatment.
Accepting an intolerable risk is poor governance, insurance doesn't transfer reputational or ethical harm, and a disclaimer doesn't meaningfully reduce the harm.
3. AI Governance and Responsible AI Leadership
A hospital is deploying AI that suggests possible diagnoses from imaging. Which oversight model is appropriate?
Human-in-the-loop: a qualified clinician reviews and makes every diagnostic decision
Human-out-of-the-loop: the AI's diagnosis goes directly to patients
High-stakes decisions affecting health, rights, or safety need a human in the loop who decides before any action.
Removing humans, relying on an accuracy threshold alone, or reacting only to complaints creates unacceptable patient-safety and liability risks.
3. AI Governance and Responsible AI Leadership

A social platform's AI automatically hides posts that violate community rules. A trust and safety team watches dashboards, samples decisions, and can reverse actions or adjust thresholds in real time. Which oversight model is this?
In human-on-the-loop oversight, the AI acts on its own while people monitor and can step in.
It suits high-volume, medium-risk decisions. Human-in-the-loop would require approval before each action, and out-of-the-loop would have no monitoring.
3. AI Governance and Responsible AI Leadership
For which use is human-out-of-the-loop automation most appropriate?
Deciding which employees to lay off
Routing incoming internal IT tickets to the correct support queue, with easy re-routing if it's wrong
Full automation fits low-risk, reversible, well-tested decisions where errors are cheap and easy to fix, like ticket routing.
Mortgages, medication, and layoffs significantly affect people and need meaningful human oversight.
3. AI Governance and Responsible AI Leadership
An insurance chatbot answers routine policy questions well but sometimes gets complex claims disputes wrong. What design best balances automation and safety?
Set escalation rules so low-confidence answers and sensitive topics, such as disputes and complaints, are routed to human agents
Raise the temperature so the chatbot tries harder
Let the chatbot handle everything and review a sample once a year
Escalation paths triggered by confidence scores, topic detection, or customer requests let AI handle routine volume while people handle complex or sensitive cases.
Removing the chatbot gives up value, temperature doesn't fix judgment, and yearly sampling is too infrequent.
3. AI Governance and Responsible AI Leadership

A bank's customer assistant must never give personalized investment advice, must block abusive language, and must mask account numbers in its responses. Which Amazon Bedrock capability is designed to enforce these rules across applications?
Amazon Bedrock Guardrails, with denied topics, content filters, and sensitive-information (PII) filters
Bedrock Guardrails applies configurable safeguards: denied topics (such as investment advice), content filters for harmful or abusive content, PII redaction, and grounding checks.
Knowledge Bases provides RAG, Provisioned Throughput is a pricing and capacity option, and Cost Explorer analyzes spending.
3. AI Governance and Responsible AI Leadership
A retailer's new AI pricing engine starts setting obviously wrong prices on popular products during a holiday weekend. What safeguard should already have been in place?
A kill switch and rollback plan to quickly disable the AI and revert to the previous pricing rules
Removing all monitoring to reduce noise
Controllability includes the ability to stop and roll back AI quickly, with a tested fallback process.
A larger model doesn't stop the current failure, marketing doesn't fix it, and removing monitoring delays detection.
3. AI Governance and Responsible AI Leadership
A generative AI tool drafts 50,000 customer emails a month, and reviewing every one isn't feasible. How should the company maintain quality oversight?
Review none, since AI is reliable
Review a statistically meaningful sample regularly, with automated checks, and increase sampling when issues appear
Human review by sampling, backed by automated quality and safety checks, scales oversight in proportion to risk and volume.
No review gives up quality assurance, full review removes the efficiency gain, and stopping gives up the value.
3. AI Governance and Responsible AI Leadership

A company requires human review of all AI credit-limit recommendations, but auditors find reviewers rarely change anything. Which TWO changes would make the oversight *meaningful*? Pick the pair of correct statements.  (1) Give reviewers the authority, time, and training to challenge and override AI recommendations.  (2) Measure reviewers only on how fast they approve.  (3) Show reviewers the AI's confidence and the key factors behind each recommendation.  (4) Hide the AI recommendation entirely.  (5) Reduce the number of reviewers to speed things up.
Meaningful oversight needs empowered, trained reviewers and enough information, such as confidence levels and explanations, to judge outputs.
Speed-only targets and fewer reviewers encourage rubber-stamping, and hiding the recommendation throws away the AI's value instead of overseeing it.
4. Business Readiness, Leadership, and AI Transformation
Before committing $5 million to an enterprise AI program, a CEO wants to understand whether the organization is prepared. What should be assessed?
Readiness across strategy and leadership, people and skills, processes, data, technology, culture, and governance
Only the size of the budget
Gaps in leadership, skills, data, culture, or governance often derail programs more than technology gaps do. Looking only at infrastructure, budget, or competitors misses most failure points.
4. Business Readiness, Leadership, and AI Transformation

A company has run six generative AI experiments across departments. None are in production, and there are no shared platforms, standards, or governance. Where is it on a typical AI maturity curve, and what's the next focus?
Transforming; focus on new business models
Scaling; expand to all departments now
Experimenting or piloting; focus on putting the best use cases into production with shared foundations and governance
Isolated experiments with nothing in production and no common foundations mark an early stage.

The next step is to operationalize: take promising use cases to production while building reusable platforms, standards, and governance. Transformation and scaling come later, and the company has already started.
4. Business Readiness, Leadership, and AI Transformation
A company uses the AWS Cloud Adoption Framework (AWS CAF) to assess AI readiness. Which perspective focuses on culture, organizational structure, leadership, and workforce skills?
AWS CAF has six perspectives: Business, People, Governance, Platform, Security, and Operations.
The People perspective covers culture, leadership, change, and skills. Platform covers technology foundations, Security covers protection, and Operations covers running workloads.
4. Business Readiness, Leadership, and AI Transformation

A readiness assessment shows a retailer has strong data but no one with experience evaluating generative AI outputs, managing AI vendors, or running AI products. What are the main ways to close this capability gap?
Combine options: train existing staff, hire key roles, and partner for near-term delivery with knowledge transfer
Ignore it, since the technology will manage itself
Only hire, and only after the program finishes
Capability gaps are usually closed with a mix of upskilling, targeted hiring, and partnering, often at the same time, while building internal ownership.
Ignoring the gap, hiring too late, or outsourcing accountability permanently all undermine success.
4. Business Readiness, Leadership, and AI Transformation

At a conservative financial firm, employees say failed projects have hurt careers in the past. Teams are reluctant to try AI experiments that might not work. What readiness issue is this, and what helps?
A data quality issue; clean the data
A culture issue; leaders should create psychological safety for well-designed experiments, reward learning, and set clear guardrails
A model size issue; buy a bigger model
A budget issue; double the IT budget
Culture is often the real blocker.
AI adoption needs experimentation within safe boundaries, so leaders must signal that disciplined experiments that "fail fast" are valued. Data, model size, and budget don't address fear of failure.
4. Business Readiness, Leadership, and AI Transformation

After assessing current AI capabilities against the target state needed for its strategy, a company has a list of gaps in skills, data platforms, and governance. What should it do with this gap analysis?
File it away for the annual report
Close every gap before starting any AI use case
Turn it into a sequenced AI roadmap that addresses foundational gaps alongside early, feasible use cases
Share it only with the IT department

Effective roadmaps build foundations, such as data, skills, and governance, *in parallel* with quick-win use cases that deliver value and fund further investment. Filing it away wastes it, waiting for perfect readiness stalls progress, and gaps span the whole business, not just IT.
4. Business Readiness, Leadership, and AI Transformation

The AWS CAF describes a transformation journey in four iterative phases. In which phase does an organization identify capability gaps and dependencies across the organization, and address stakeholder concerns, to build an action plan?
The AWS CAF phases are Envision, Align, Launch, and Scale.

In Envision you identify transformation opportunities tied to business outcomes. In Align you find capability gaps, dependencies, and stakeholder concerns. In Launch you deliver pilots that show value, and in Scale you expand them to the desired scope.
4. Business Readiness, Leadership, and AI Transformation

Readiness assessments often focus too much on technology. Which TWO *non-technical* factors are among the strongest predictors of AI program success? Pick the pair of correct statements.  (1) The brand of laptops employees use.  (2) Visible executive sponsorship and leadership commitment.  (3) The number of AI vendors that have pitched to the company.  (4) Workforce skills and a culture open to change and experimentation.  (5) The age of the company's logo.
Leadership commitment, and people with a supportive culture, consistently decide whether AI programs succeed.
Laptop brands, vendor pitches, and logos are irrelevant to readiness.
4. Business Readiness, Leadership, and AI Transformation

A company has four AI use cases in production with monitoring and a basic governance process. Each one was built separately, with its own data pipelines, prompts, and guardrails, which slows every new project. What's the logical next step in its AI maturity?
Return to experimenting with new proofs of concept
Replace all four use cases with one large model
Move toward scaling by building shared, reusable components (data pipelines, guardrails, prompt libraries, evaluation tools) and standard processes
Moving from "operationalizing" to "scaling" means turning one-off builds into reusable platforms and standards, so each new use case is faster and cheaper.
Going back to experiments or stopping loses momentum, and a single model doesn't solve the platform and process gap.
4. Business Readiness, Leadership, and AI Transformation
Which AWS Cloud Adoption Framework (AWS CAF) perspective helps ensure that AI and cloud investments speed up business outcomes, through strategy, portfolio management, and business cases?
The Business perspective ties technology investments to business outcomes through strategy, product and portfolio management, and value measurement.
Platform covers technical foundations, Operations covers running workloads, and Security covers protection.
4. Business Readiness, Leadership, and AI Transformation

A telecom company wants AI to predict which customers will cancel. Customer profiles live in the CRM, billing history in a separate finance system, and support tickets in a third tool, and the systems don't share customer IDs. What's the main readiness problem?
The foundation model is too small
Data silos prevent a unified customer view; the data must be integrated and matched before the AI can use it effectively
The company has too much data
Data silos are one of the most common blockers to AI value.
Predicting cancellations needs a combined view across systems with consistent identifiers. Model size, data volume, and Region aren't the issue.
4. Business Readiness, Leadership, and AI Transformation

Three AI projects at a retailer keep failing because product attributes are inconsistent and outdated. When asked who maintains product data, each department points to another. What foundational step addresses the root cause?
Buy a larger AI model that can handle messy data
Have each AI project clean the product data separately
Assign clear data ownership and stewardship, with accountable owners and day-to-day stewards, plus quality standards
Stop using product data in AI
Without ownership, data quality decays and every project pays to clean the same data again.

Data governance roles, an owner who is accountable and stewards who maintain quality, fix the cause. Bigger models don't fix bad data, cleaning separately duplicates effort, and avoiding the data gives up value.
4. Business Readiness, Leadership, and AI Transformation
Analysts at an insurer spend weeks finding out which data sets exist, what fields mean, and whether the data can be trusted before every AI project. What would help most?
A data catalog: a searchable inventory of data assets with descriptions, owners, quality notes, and access information
Asking IT to email data sets on request
A data catalog makes data discoverable, understandable, and trustworthy, cutting the time it takes to start AI work.
Printed spreadsheets and email requests don't scale, and a model's context window has nothing to do with finding data.
4. Business Readiness, Leadership, and AI Transformation
An auditor asks a bank where the data used to train its credit model came from, and what transformations were applied before training. Which data capability answers this?
Data lineage: tracking the data's origin and every change it went through
Data lineage records where data came from and how it changed.
It's essential for auditability, debugging, and regulatory trust in AI. Compression is about storage, temperature is a generation setting, and minimization limits what data is used.
4. Business Readiness, Leadership, and AI Transformation

A company plans a RAG assistant over its internal document repository. A sample review finds many outdated policies, several conflicting versions of the same document, and draft files mixed with final ones. What should happen before launch?
Launch now; the model will work out which version is correct
Curate the source content: remove or archive outdated and duplicate documents, mark authoritative versions, and assign content owners to keep it current
Raise the temperature to handle ambiguity
Fine-tune the model on all the documents, including the drafts
RAG answers are only as good as the documents retrieved.

Conflicting or stale content produces confident wrong answers. Data readiness for generative AI includes curating unstructured content and giving it owners. The model can't reliably pick the right version, temperature doesn't help, and fine-tuning on drafts makes things worse.
4. Business Readiness, Leadership, and AI Transformation
A retailer wants AI to adjust promotions daily based on stock levels, but inventory data is loaded into its analytics platform only once a quarter. Which data-quality dimension is the problem?
Timeliness means data is current enough for its purpose.
Daily decisions can't rely on quarterly data, so the data pipeline must be updated to refresh more often. The data may well be accurate, complete, and free of duplicates and still be too old to use.
4. Business Readiness, Leadership, and AI Transformation

Which TWO characteristics show that a data set is *ready* to support an AI use case? Pick the pair of correct statements.  (1) It's accessible to the AI solution through secure, appropriate permissions.  (2) It's stored only on one employee's laptop.  (3) It has documented quality, definitions, and a known owner.  (4) It's a copy that hasn't been updated in three years.  (5) It's spread across personal email attachments.
AI-ready data is accessible under proper controls, understood (with definitions and documented quality), and governed (with an owner).
A laptop-only copy, stale data, or data scattered across email attachments is neither accessible nor trustworthy.
4. Business Readiness, Leadership, and AI Transformation

A company expects its AI workloads to grow, but it's unsure by how much. The IT director proposes spending $4 million upfront on on-premises GPU servers. What's the stronger infrastructure approach for this uncertainty?
Buy twice as many servers to be safe
Delay all AI until demand is known
Build a private data center for AI only
Use scalable cloud and managed AI services that grow with demand on a pay-as-you-go basis, adding commitments once usage stabilizes
With uncertain demand, elastic cloud resources and managed services avoid large upfront bets and idle capacity.
Savings Plans or provisioned capacity can be added once usage becomes predictable. Overbuying, delaying, or building a data center all lock in cost or give up value.
4. Business Readiness, Leadership, and AI Transformation

An organization wants a central, scalable place to store structured and unstructured data of any type, such as documents, images, logs, and tables, as a foundation for analytics and AI on AWS. What is this commonly called, and which service typically underpins it?
A data lake, typically built on Amazon S3
A spreadsheet, built on Amazon Polly
A chatbot, built on Amazon Lex
A data silo, built on personal drives
A data lake centralizes raw data of any type at scale, and on AWS it's commonly built on Amazon S3, a common foundation for analytics and AI.
Polly is text-to-speech, Lex builds chatbots, and silos are the problem a data lake helps solve.
4. Business Readiness, Leadership, and AI Transformation

A CIO says, "No AI projects until our three-year enterprise data platform program is finished, because our data isn't ready." Meanwhile, two high-value use cases need only a few data sets that could be cleaned within two months. What's the best recommendation?
Agree, and pause all AI for three years
Prepare the specific data the priority use cases need now, deliver value, and feed the lessons and requirements into the broader data platform program
Launch AI on the current, uncleaned data immediately
Cancel the data platform program and focus only on AI
Data readiness can grow step by step, use case by use case.

Fixing the data that high-value use cases need delivers value early and guides the larger platform work. Waiting three years gives up value, using unclean data invites failure, and cancelling the platform program sacrifices long-term foundations.
4. Business Readiness, Leadership, and AI Transformation
Research on AI programs consistently identifies one role as among the strongest predictors of success. Which role is it, and what does it do?
An external vendor who writes the code
A junior analyst who documents meetings
An executive sponsor who champions the initiative, secures funding, removes roadblocks, and signals its importance
A help-desk agent who answers user questions
Executive sponsors give AI programs authority, resources, cross-functional alignment, and visible commitment, which are critical for overcoming resistance and scaling.
The other roles matter, but they can't provide that organizational leverage.
4. Business Readiness, Leadership, and AI Transformation
After an AI document-processing tool is announced, back-office staff fear for their jobs. Some quietly avoid using it. What's the most effective leadership response?
Require usage and monitor every keystroke
Say nothing and hope the fear fades
Promise that no role will ever change, even if that isn't true
Communicate openly how roles will change, involve staff in redesigning the work, and offer reskilling paths toward higher-value tasks
Resistance often comes from uncertainty and fear.

Honest, transparent communication, involving staff in the redesign, and real reskilling investment build trust and adoption. Coercion breeds hidden resistance, silence feeds rumors, and false promises damage credibility.
4. Business Readiness, Leadership, and AI Transformation
A global company wants adoption of its new AI assistant to spread across 40 offices. A central training team alone can't reach everyone effectively. Which approach helps most?
An AI champions network: enthusiastic, trained employees in each team who model usage, share tips, and gather feedback
A mandate with penalties for non-use
Waiting for employees to discover the tool themselves
Peer champions inside teams spread practical know-how, build credibility, and surface feedback, and peer influence often beats top-down mandates.
One email doesn't change behavior, penalties breed resentment, and passive discovery leads to low adoption.
